before: The study examines whether matching one melt-pool length also constrains fusion shape and the rear thermal interval in a conduction model. One source factor is fitted to condition B length. Width and depth are excluded from the fit, and conditions A and C retain the fitted factor. A four-corner comparison at B then changes the high-temperature conductivity and sensible-storage continuations independently. The rear solidus and liquidus positions resolve whether these changes displace the thermal tail or widen the phase interval; their separation and scan speed define a material passage time.
after: The analysis connects surface-length calibration, fusion-zone shape and the rear phase interval through two complementary comparisons. A source factor fitted to condition B length is retained for all three operating conditions and for width and depth. At B, independent changes in the high-temperature conductivity and sensible-storage continuations resolve their contributions to the calibrated field. Rear solidus and liquidus positions then separate thermal-tail displacement from phase-span change, while scan speed converts the spatial interval to material passage time.

Sensible specific heat decreases from 721.13 to 670~\si{\joule\per\kilogram\per\kelvin}, or 7.09\%. With the latent contribution included, effective specific heat decreases from 5387.79 to 5336.67~\si{\joule\per\kilogram\per\kelvin}, or 0.95\%, and enthalpy from the cold reference decreases by 0.66\%. This matched-temperature comparison describes the adopted mushy interval. A retained local face P\'eclet diagnostic for the mushy $\xi$ faces increases in median from 4.44 in LL to 5.77 in HL, consistent with reduced diffusion relative to coordinate enthalpy transport. The diagnostic is consistent with a conductivity-dependent shift in the model's transport balance. The corresponding retained rear hot-region outward diffusive flux rises from 14.724 to 14.913~W. Since that region is selected by temperature and changes with the solved state, conductivity holding cannot be equated with a measured reduction in its integrated outward heat flow. The branch also changes surface recovery consistently with $k$.
after: At 1320~$^\circ$C, conductivity changes from 32.51 to 25.20~\si{\watt\per\metre\per\kelvin} under holding, a reduction of 22.48\%. Sensible specific heat decreases from 721.13 to 670~\si{\joule\per\kilogram\per\kelvin}, or 7.09\%. With latent storage included, effective specific heat decreases from 5387.79 to 5336.67~\si{\joule\per\kilogram\per\kelvin}, or 0.95\%, and enthalpy from the cold reference decreases by 0.66\%. The property changes therefore perturb transport and storage by different amounts in the adopted mushy interval. The median axial-face P\'eclet diagnostic rises from 4.44 in LL to 5.77 in HL, indicating a changed balance of diffusion and coordinate enthalpy transport on the selected faces. Integrated outward diffusion from the rear hot region also rises, from 14.724 to 14.913~W. Both the gradients and the temperature-selected integration boundary change with the solution, so this regional flux requires interpretation together with its moving spatial population. The conductivity branch also changes surface recovery through the corresponding material primitive.

The retained B width excess and depth deficit, together with the B--C shape response, locate its remaining discrepancy in transverse heat distribution and penetration (Fig.~\ref{fig:comparison}). Surface length supplies one constraint on this field; fusion shape and temperature trajectories supply additional information. Source representation, transport closure and the relation between radiance-derived and temperature-threshold boundaries therefore enter the assessment as distinct contributors.

before: Keeping the calibrated source fixed reveals opposing property responses that a joint replacement would conceal. Conductivity holding extends the pool at either storage setting, while sensible-storage holding shortens it at either conductivity setting (Table~\ref{tab:factorial}). Their combination produces a 34.28~\um{} length increase, with the interaction modifying the magnitudes. The rear profiles locate the dominant response: the rear solidus accounts for 98.3\% of the conductivity-induced length increase, and the liquidus moves almost the same distance. The principal change is a displacement of the thermal tail relative to the source, rather than comparable widening of the rear phase interval (Fig.~\ref{fig:factorial}). None of the four corners removes the B wide/shallow discrepancy.
after: Keeping the calibrated source fixed separates opposing property responses. before: A discriminating thermal test would retain a defined source and observation mapping, reserve tracks or profiles before fitting, and compare an excluded temperature trajectory together with width and depth. Composition- and state-matched high-temperature property evidence would address which continuation is physically appropriate; a matched thermal trajectory would address whether the calibrated field is credible. Until those tests are available, the result is specific but useful: one geometric fit leaves distinct questions about fusion shape, tail position, phase separation and material cooling time, and the fixed-source continuation contrast reveals which of those questions the assumed properties influence.
after: The comparisons identify complementary evidence for the next assessment. A defined source and observation mapping, tracks or profiles reserved before fitting, and an independently measured temperature trajectory would test the calibrated field together with its width and depth. Composition- and state-matched high-temperature data would constrain the material continuation. Each observation addresses a different part of the interpretation: fusion shape assesses energy redistribution, rear boundaries locate the phase interval, and a temperature history assesses its passage in material time. The present fixed-source contrasts supply this separation within the assumed conduction balance.
purpose: Develop the observed relation and its assessment consequence in objective prose.

before: Geometric calibration provides a useful constraint on thermal modeling, but its solidification meaning depends on the properties and observables used to interpret the fitted field. For the present IN625 enthalpy model, the source factor fitted to a surface length leaves a width excess of 19.54~\um{} and a depth deficit of 4.88~\um{}. The faster fixed-source condition remains wide and shallow. The excluded shape quantities therefore supply information that the length fit does not capture.
after: Geometric calibration is useful for low-cost thermal modeling of laser processing, while its physical assessment requires the observables carried by the fitted field to be distinguished. In the present IN625 enthalpy calculation, a close surface-length fit coexists with a wider and shallower fusion envelope than the reference means. The fixed-power speed comparison further exposes a discrepancy in the balance between transverse contraction and penetration. Fusion shape consequently provides an assessment of energy redistribution beyond the fitted axial extent.
purpose: Develop the observed relation and its assessment consequence in objective prose.

before: The fixed-source property contrast separates opposing responses that a joint continuation change conceals. Conductivity holding lengthens the pool by 43.21~\um{}, sensible heat-capacity holding shortens it by 6.17~\um{}, and their interaction gives a joint extension of 34.28~\um{}. Rear solidus displacement accounts for 98.3\% of the conductivity-induced extension, while the rear phase separation changes much less. The dominant response is displacement of the thermal tail, with opposing depth effects that do not resolve the geometric discrepancy.
after: Independent continuation contrasts reveal how high-temperature transport and storage assumptions contribute to that field. Conductivity holding extends the pool and sensible heat-capacity holding shortens it at both tested factor levels, giving a joint length increase of 34.28~\um{}. Rear solidus and liquidus translation dominates the conductivity response, while their separation changes comparatively little. The principal sensitivity therefore concerns the location of the thermal tail; the retained width/depth discrepancy calls for additional source, transport and observation evidence.

before: Spatial phase separation and material cooling time must also be distinguished. Rear spans near 80~\um{} at 0.8 and 1.2~m/s correspond to passage times of 100.33 and 67.33~\us{} and a 49.02\% difference in the interval-mean cooling rate. These are transformations of the modeled centerline field. Together, the results show why thermal interpretation after a geometric fit requires separate assessment of fusion shape, property response and material time. Aligned source and observation definitions, credible high-temperature data and an independent thermal profile are needed to test that interpretation physically.
after: Material cooling time adds a further constraint to this spatial interpretation. Almost equal rear phase spans at 0.8 and 1.2~m/s correspond to a roughly one-third reduction in passage time and a 49.02\% increase in the modeled interval-mean cooling rate. The relation follows from passage through the same quasi-steady field and defines a derived centerline history. Taken together, the comparisons distinguish fusion shape, tail position and material time as complementary targets for thermal-model assessment. Credible high-temperature material data and a temperature trajectory aligned with the source, phase interval and observation definitions would establish their physical correspondence.
purpose: Develop the observed relation and its assessment consequence in objective prose.
